query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a low-level yttrium (Y) dopant into the surface of boride‐based components (e.g., via a Y-containing conversion coating) will promote the rapid formation of a tightly adherent, Al2O3‐rich interfacial layer during hot-dip aluminum plating, thereby reducing molten-aluminum corrosion relative to untreated boride surfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment without reactive element modifications.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment that introduces a small concentration of yttrium onto the boride component surface (for example, through a Y-containing conversion coating or surface doping process).
generation.conditions: Under typical hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (molten aluminum at about 660°C, in an atmosphere free from aggressive species such as high chlorides or excessive oxidizers), with dopant levels kept low to avoid over-modification.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation and retention of a continuous, adherent Al2O3-rich interfacial barrier, with yttrium segregating at grain boundaries and the metal-oxide interface to improve oxide adhesion.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium is known to have a reactive element effect—by segregating at critical interfaces it reduces oxide scale spallation and impedes the inward/outward diffusion of species. In this case, it facilitates the formation of a protective alumina layer that serves as an effective diffusion barrier against molten aluminum attack on the boride substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated components, the Y-doped boride surfaces will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates during molten-aluminum exposure, as indicated by reduced weight loss and decreased oxide spallation or corrosion penetration.
generation.baseline: The corrosion performance (e.g., weight loss, oxide scale spallation area) of untreated boride-based components when subjected to standard hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a specific range of Y concentrations (too high could be detrimental) and under process conditions typical of hot-dip plating (~660°C, controlled atmosphere). Deviations from these conditions or excessive dopant levels may negate the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., exact percentage reduction in weight loss) is not predetermined and will require experimental optimization to establish the ideal Y concentration and treatment protocol.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based samples. One set receives the yttrium-doping surface treatment (e.g., via a Y-containing conversion coating) while the control set remains untreated. Subject both sets to immersion in molten aluminum at approximately 660°C for a fixed duration (e.g., 60 hours) under identical, controlled environmental conditions.
measurements: Weight loss per unit area after treatment
Surface and cross-sectional analysis of oxide scale morphology and adhesion (via SEM/EDS)
Depth of corrosion penetration assessed by microstructural examination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant (e.g., >10%) reduction in weight loss, oxide spallation area, or corrosion penetration compared to the untreated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA.
